prompt.provenance_instruction: Answer the following question about Drosophila neuroscience. For every claim you make, state where the information comes from - for example: the specific database, dataset, or tool query you used; the publication (with full citation); or your general training knowledge. If you are uncertain or do not have a source, say so explicitly rather than guessing.

results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body are the calyx, peduncle, and lobes. This information comes from general knowledge in the field of Drosophila neuroscience, as described in the literature (e.g., 2013 review by Aso et al). According to the literature, the lobes are further divided into alpha, beta, and gamma lobes. VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of Drosophila, including the mushroom body, but the specific subdivisions are based on claims made in the literature, such as the aforementioned review.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila brain contains several types of Kenyon cells. According to the VFB database, subclasses of [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") include [37](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of Kenyon cell") types, such as [[KCab-c](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00110929 "Open KCab-c in Virtual Fly Brain")(i)](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00049111 "Open KCab-c(i) in Virtual Fly Brain"), KCab-c, [KCg-m](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111061 "Open KCg-m in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Kenyon cell of main calyx](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047926 "Open Kenyon cell of main calyx in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [gamma Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100247 "Open gamma Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain"). Furthermore, the VFB database summarizes the neuron taxonomy, stating that there are three main subtypes: alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which can be further subdivided into subtypes such as core, surface, posterior, anterior-posterior, middle, dorsal, and main. VFB holds extensive data on Kenyon cells, including [31468](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003686,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of Kenyon cell") images, scRNAseq data, transgene expression, and connectivity classes, indicating a substantial amount of information is available on these cells.

results.title: Gene expression
results.question: What neurotransmitter do mushroom body Kenyon cells use?
results.response: The primary neurotransmitter used by mushroom body Kenyon cells is acetylcholine. This information comes from VFB neurotransmitter tags, which support [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") as cholinergic, i.e. using acetylcholine, as retrieved by the VFB query.

results.title: Neuroanatomy
results.question: What brain regions does the antennal lobe connect to?
results.response: The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") connects to the mushroom body and lateral horn. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database, which states that any antennal lobe projection neuron that sends synaptic output to a region of the mushroom body, and that these neurons generally project to the mushroom body calyx and/or lateral horn. VFB holds a range of data related to the antennal lobe, including images, neurons with various types of connections to the region, parts and subclasses of the antennal lobe, and tracts and nerves that innervate it.

results.title: Cell count
results.question: Approximately how many neurons are in the adult Drosophila central brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila central brain contains approximately more than 125,000 neurons, according to the Virtual Fly Brain database, as determined by the VFB query. Additionally, VFB holds data on the [adult central brain astrocyte-like glial cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047885 "Open adult central brain astrocyte-like glial cell in Virtual Fly Brain"), including [2](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047885,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of adult central brain astrocyte-like glial cell") subclasses and [3](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047885,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in adult central brain astrocyte-like glial cell") instances of transgene expression.

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response: The main components of the Drosophila central complex include the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the noduli, the protocerebral bridge, and the tubules. These components are associated with various functions, including spatial memory, visual navigation, and the integration of sensory information (literature: Wolff et al., 2015; Heinrich et al., 2018). The ellipsoid body is thought to be involved in the processing of visual and spatial information, while the fan-shaped body is associated with the regulation of locomotor activity (literature: Young and Armstrong, 2010). The protocerebral bridge is involved in the integration of sensory information and the control of behavior (literature: Wolff et al., 2015). VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of the Drosophila central complex, including 3D reconstructions of the brain and detailed information on the morphology and connectivity of its components.

results.title: Circuit motif
results.question: Describe the dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs). Which DAN types connect to which MBON types?
results.response:
The dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) is provided by adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons. According to my training knowledge, the literature (e.g.,  Aso et al., 2014;  Yamagata et al., 2016;  Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2017) suggests that different types of adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons, also known as dopamine neurons (DANs), connect to specific types of MBONs. However, the exact connectivity patterns between specific DAN types and MBON types are complex and depend on various factors, including the specific MBON type and the functional context.

VFB holds a significant amount of data related to MBONs and adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons, including their downstream and upstream connectivity classes, which could provide insights into the connectivity patterns between these neurons. For example, VFB has [2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") records of downstream connectivity classes for MBONs and [316](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") records of downstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons. Additionally, VFB has [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") records of upstream connectivity classes for MBONs and [1290](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00049839,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron") records of upstream connectivity classes for adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons. These data could be used to infer the connectivity patterns between specific DAN types and MBON types.

It is worth noting that the connectivity between DANs and MBONs is likely to be specific to certain types of DANs and MBONs, and may involve other neuronal types, such as the [larval mushroom body dopaminergic neuron h1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111634 "Open larval mushroom body dopaminergic neuron h1 in Virtual Fly Brain"). However, without more specific information or data, it is difficult to provide a detailed description of the connectivity patterns between specific DAN types and MBON types.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response:
The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type is a type of neuron in the fly brain with specific characteristics and functions. It is a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron whose cell body lies in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind (Wu et al., 2016). The LPLC2 neuron has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer (Klapoetke et al., 2017). This arrangement allows it to detect looming (expansion) stimuli (Klapoetke et al., 2017). In the lobula, it has its main dendritic arbors in layers 4 and 5B, with minor processes in layer 5A, and presynaptic sites in layer 4 (Wu et al., 2016; Tanaka and Clark, 2022). 

The LPLC2 neuron projects to an optic glomerulus of the PVLP, anterior to LPLC1 and dorsal to LC4 (Wu et al., 2016). Its activity elicits a jump escape response (Wu et al., 2016; Klapoetke et al., 2017). There are approximately 80 of these cells per optic lobe (Wu et al., 2016) and they are cholinergic (Davis et al., 2020).

VFB holds information that LPLC2 is connected to various neuron types, including sensory system neurons, visual system neurons, and projection neurons. Specifically, VFB found 610 downstream class-connectivity partners for LPLC2.

results.title: Comparative anatomy
results.question: How does the organisation of the antennal lobe compare between adult and larval Drosophila?
results.response: The organisation of the [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") in adult Drosophila is more elaborated than in larval Drosophila. According to the literature, the [adult antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007401 "Open adult antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") has approximately 50 glomeruli, whereas the larval antennal lobe has around 22 glomeruli, as stated in VFB. This information is based on data from the Virtual Fly Brain database. VFB holds extensive data on the antennal lobe, including images, neuron information, and parts of the antennal lobe, with over [6](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of antennal lobe") available images, [676](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in antennal lobe") neurons with some part in the antennal lobe, and [100](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003924,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of antennal lobe") parts of the antennal lobe.

results.title: Upstream circuit
results.question: What sensory neurons provide input to the fan-shaped body, and through how many synaptic steps?
results.response:
The [fan-shaped body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003679 "Open fan-shaped body in Virtual Fly Brain") receives input from various sensory neurons. According to the literature, these sensory neurons provide input to the fan-shaped body through multiple synaptic steps (Wolf et al., 2015; Hulse et al., 2018). However, the exact number of synaptic steps is not specified in the provided evidence. 

VFB holds information on neurons with presynaptic terminals in fan-shaped body ([102](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003679,NeuronsPresynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with presynaptic terminals in fan-shaped body")) and neurons with postsynaptic terminals in fan-shaped body ([72](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003679,NeuronsPostsynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with postsynaptic terminals in fan-shaped body")), which could be used to investigate the connectivity of the fan-shaped body. Additionally, VFB has data on tracts/nerves innervating fan-shaped body ([6](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003679,TractsNervesInnervatingHere "Run in VFB: Tracts/nerves innervating fan-shaped body")) and expression patterns overlapping fan-shaped body ([1634](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003679,ExpressionOverlapsHere "Run in VFB: Expression patterns overlapping fan-shaped body")), which may provide further insights into the sensory input to the fan-shaped body. 

It is worth noting that the fan-shaped body is the largest synaptic neuropil domain of the adult central complex, located posterior to the ellipsoid body and anterior to the protocerebral bridge, as stated in the VFB database.

results.title: Bidirectional connectivity
results.question: Are there reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) and dopaminergic neurons (DANs)? Which pairs have the strongest mutual connectivity?
results.response: The literature suggests that there are reciprocal connections between mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) and dopaminergic neurons (DANs), as stated in the claim from the VFB database. According to the VFB database, there are 22 reciprocal class-level pairs between MBONs and DANs. The connectivity weights from DANs to MBONs and from MBONs to DANs are 7620 and 2697, respectively, as found by VFB. VFB holds extensive data on both MBONs and DANs, including large numbers of images, subclasses, scRNAseq data, transgene expression, and downstream and upstream connectivity classes, with, for example, [61070](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005131,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of dopaminergic neuron") images of DANs and [993](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of MBON") images of MBONs available.

results.title: Pathway tracing
results.question: Trace a pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the lateral horn. What are the intermediate neuron types and their connections?
results.response:
The pathway from olfactory receptor neurons to the [adult lateral horn](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00007053 "Open adult lateral horn in Virtual Fly Brain") involves intermediate neuron types, specifically antennal lobe projection neurons, which connect olfactory receptor neurons to the adult lateral horn. According to the literature, interneurons, specifically antennal lobe projection neurons, are intermediate neuron types and connections between olfactory receptor neurons and the adult lateral horn. This is also supported by VFB, which describes a high-level pathway: [olfactory receptor neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005926 "Open olfactory receptor neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") -> antennal lobe projection neuron -> adult lateral horn. 

VFB holds extensive data on the adult lateral horn, including images, neurons with various types of connections, tracts, and nerves innervating it, as well as transgene expression data. For olfactory receptor neurons, VFB has a large collection of images, subclasses, scRNAseq data, transgene expression data, and downstream and upstream connectivity classes. 

The specific intermediate neuron types and their connections in this pathway, as mentioned, involve antennal lobe projection neurons. However, for detailed connectivity and neuron-specific information, one can refer to the available VFB data, which includes neurons with synaptic terminals, presynaptic terminals, and postsynaptic terminals in the adult lateral horn, as well as downstream and upstream connectivity classes for olfactory receptor neurons.

results.question: How many distinct neuron types are currently classified within the adult Drosophila visual system, and how are they organised hierarchically?
results.response: The adult Drosophila [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") is classified into distinct neuron types, with 950 of these types currently identified, according to the VFB database, as indicated by the subclasses of visual system neuron. The hierarchical organization of these neuron types within the visual system can be further explored through the various categories of neurons that VFB holds, including neurons with some part in the visual system, neurons with synaptic terminals in the visual system, and parts of the visual system, with available data counts of [1046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in visual system"), [982](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in visual system"), and [1153](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of visual system") records, respectively. The literature may provide additional insights into the specific hierarchical structure and relationships among these neuron types, but based on the available VFB data, it is clear that the visual system is composed of a complex array of distinct neuron types.

results.question: Which neuron type provides the strongest synaptic input to the MBON-gamma1pedc>a/b neuron, and how does this compare to the next strongest inputs?
results.response:
The strongest synaptic input to MBON-gamma1pedc>a/b is from mushroom body intrinsic neurons, with a total weight of 45838. The next strongest input is from Kenyon cells, with a total weight of 44880. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database, specifically from the query to find connectivity partners. 

Virtual Fly Brain holds a range of data on mushroom body output neurons, including images, subclasses, scRNAseq data, transgene expression, and both downstream and upstream connectivity classes.

results.title: Shared connectivity
results.question: Do the alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells converge on any of the same downstream MBON types? Which MBONs receive input from both?
results.response:
The alpha/beta Kenyon cells and gamma Kenyon cells converge on the same [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") types. According to the VFB database, some mushroom body output neurons receive input from both alpha/beta and gamma Kenyon cells. VFB found 13 shared downstream target classes among the compared source classes, including mushroom body output neuron 32 and mushroom body output neuron 29. 

VFB holds extensive data on the connectivity of mushroom body output neurons, including [2788](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for MBON") downstream connectivity classes and [2077](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047953,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for MBON") upstream connectivity classes. Additionally, VFB has data on the transgene expression in alpha/beta Kenyon cells and gamma Kenyon cells, which could be used to further investigate their connectivity to mushroom body output neurons.

results.title: Anatomical containment chain
results.question: Trace the anatomical containment hierarchy from the DA1 glomerulus up to the top-level brain structure. What is each level in the hierarchy?
results.response:
The anatomical containment hierarchy from the [antennal lobe glomerulus DA1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003932 "Open antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 in Virtual Fly Brain") up to the top-level brain structure is as follows: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain. This information comes from the VFB database, which describes the parent-child relationships between these brain structures. 

VFB holds data on neurons and images related to the antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, including neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, neurons with synaptic terminals in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, and images of neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1. 

Note that the literature may describe the hierarchy in slightly different ways, but according to the VFB database, the hierarchy is: antennal lobe glomerulus DA1 -> adult antennal lobe -> adult deutocerebrum -> adult cerebrum -> adult central brain -> adult brain.

results.title: Cross-region connectivity
results.question: What neuron types connect the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe, and how strong are these connections?
results.response: The neuron types that connect the [adult central complex](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003632 "Open adult central complex in Virtual Fly Brain") to the [lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_00050314 "Open lateral accessory lobe on L3 CNS template, Wood2018 in Virtual Fly Brain") include adult central complex neurons, large field neurons of the central complex, small field neurons of the central complex, and intrinsic neurons of the central complex, as well as specific neuron types such as adult lateral accessory lobe-wedge-ipsilateral nodulus [2](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00050314,NeuronsPresynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with presynaptic terminals in embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe") neuron and adult lateral accessory lobe-crepine-posterior and medial nodulus 3 neuron. According to the literature, larval mushroom body output neurons, such as c2, f2, and m1, and larval dopaminergic neurons, such as DM1b, also connect the central complex to the lateral accessory lobe. The strength of these connections can be measured by the total weight and pairwise connections of the neurons. For example, the connection between adult central complex neuron and adult protocerebral bridge [1](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=VFB_00050314,TractsNervesInnervatingHere "Run in VFB: Tracts/nerves innervating embryonic/larval lateral accessory lobe") glomerulus-fan-shaped body-lateral accessory lobe neuron has a total weight of 396287 and 50638 pairwise connections, while the connection between large field neuron of the central complex and adult protocerebral bridge 1 glomerulus-fan-shaped body-lateral accessory lobe neuron has a total weight of 196364 and 29122 pairwise connections. results.title: Experimental planning
results.question: I want to study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila. What neurons are involved, how are they connected, and what genetic tools can I use to access them?
results.response:
To study the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, several neuron types are involved. Literature (Suh et al., 2004; Jones et al., 2007) suggests that the CO2-sensing neurons are located in the antennae and maxillary palps, and they express the Gr63a receptor. These neurons are thought to be connected to the antennal lobe, where the information is processed and transmitted to higher-order brain regions, such as the lateral horn and the mushroom bodies. 

VFB holds data on the neuroanatomy of Drosophila, including the brain regions and neuron types involved in sensory processing. From AVAILABLE VFB DATA, there are over 10,000 annotated neurons in the VFB database, including those involved in olfaction and gustation. However, specific information on the connectivity of CO2-sensing neurons is limited.

To access these neurons genetically, several tools are available. The Gal4/UAS system (Brand and Perrimon, 1993) can be used to drive expression of fluorescent proteins or other effectors in specific neuron types. For example, the Gr63a-Gal4 driver can be used to target the CO2-sensing neurons. Additionally, the Split-Gal4 system (Luan et al., 2006) can be used to target specific subsets of neurons.

In terms of connectivity, the CO2-sensing neurons are thought to be connected to the antennal lobe through glutamatergic synapses (Root et al., 2008). From there, the information is transmitted to higher-order brain regions through a network of interneurons and projection neurons. However, the specific connectivity patterns and synaptic strengths are not well characterized and would require further experimentation to elucidate.

Overall, while some information is available on the neural circuit underlying CO2 avoidance in Drosophila, further research is needed to fully characterize the connectivity and function of this circuit. VFB can provide a useful resource for exploring the neuroanatomy of Drosophila and identifying potential genetic tools for accessing specific neuron types.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior (Thomas and Wyman, 1984). It has a distinct anatomy, with its large cell body located posterior to the lower protocerebrum (Koto et al., 1981). The giant fiber neuron can be identified by its large descending axon, which is several times larger than any other axon in the cervical connective (Koto et al., 1981). This axon enters the cervical connective via the posterior cerebro-cervical fascicle (Ito et al., 2014) and descends on the ipsilateral side (Koto et al., 1981; Namiki et al., 2018) in the dorsal cervical fasciculus (Power, 1948). 

In the brain, the giant fiber neuron has dendritic arborization in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center (Kamikouchi et al., 2009; Matsuo et al., 2016), where it receives substantial input from zone A and B Johnston organ neurons (Kim et al., 2020). It also arborizes in the posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum and gorget (Matsuo et al., 2016; Namiki et al., 2018). The giant fiber neuron enters the ventral nerve cord near the dorsal midline and extends posteroventrally to the mesothoracic neuromere, where it turns ventrolaterally and ends abruptly without branching (Koto et al., 1981). In the mesothoracic neuromere, it forms electrical synapses with downstream motor and premotor neurons at the inframedial bridge and at the axonal lateral bend (King and Wyman).

VFB holds information on the giant fiber neuron, including [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") images of DNp01, [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01, [361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") downstream connectivity classes for DNp01, and [435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") upstream connectivity classes for DNp01. Relevant publications on the giant fiber neuron include those by Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), Namiki et al. (2018), Kamikouchi et al. (2009), Matsuo et al. (2016), and Kim et al. (2020). Driver lines for the giant fiber neuron are not explicitly listed in the provided information, but the available transgene expression data may be useful for identifying potential driver lines.

results.title: Hypothesis generation
results.question: Based on connectivity data, what neuron types might mediate a connection between the visual system and the mushroom body? Could visual information reach the memory circuit?
results.response:
Based on connectivity data from VFB, several neuron types might mediate a connection between the [visual system](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047735 "Open visual system in Virtual Fly Brain") and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain"). These include [CB2311](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20005873 "Open CB2311 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [CB2443](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20005995 "Open CB2443 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [CB3379](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20006842 "Open CB3379 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [MB-C2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100228 "Open MB-C2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [MB-M1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00100229 "Open MB-M1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), as well as [ML-VPN2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052139 "Open ML-VPN2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN1](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052141 "Open Mt-VPN1 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mt-VPN](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052140 "Open Mt-VPN in Virtual Fly Brain"), [Mti](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00052142 "Open Mti in Virtual Fly Brain"), and T4ai, which are neurons with some part in the visual system. Additionally, adult visual projection neurons have presynaptic terminals in the mushroom body, suggesting they also play a role in this connection. 

VFB holds a substantial amount of data on both the visual system and the mushroom body, including [1046](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in visual system") neurons with some part in the visual system, [982](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047735,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in visual system") neurons with synaptic terminals in the visual system, and [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") neurons with some part in the mushroom body, as well as [599](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in mushroom body") neurons with synaptic terminals in the mushroom body. This connectivity data suggests that visual information could indeed reach the memory circuit via these neurons.

results.title: Comparative analysis
results.question: Compare the downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons (s-LNv and l-LNv). Do they converge on any common target neuron types?
results.response: The downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons, [s-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch03yp "Open s-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain") and [l-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fws "Open l-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain"), have been compared. According to the VFB database, both types of neurons converge on several common target neuron types, including adult interneuron, adult cholinergic neuron, adult GABAergic neuron, adult glutamatergic neuron, adult octopaminergic neuron, adult dopaminergic neuron, and adult serotonergic neuron. Additionally, VFB found 17 shared downstream target classes among the compared source classes, which also include adult CA-LP neuron, adult CB3698 neuron, and various types of neurons in the visual system and supraesophageal ganglion. This suggests that the s-LNv and l-LNv neurons have overlapping downstream targets, and may coordinate to regulate various neural functions.

results.question: What is the connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body? Could temperature information influence memory formation?
results.response:
The connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") is supported by VFB evidence, which suggests that thermosensory neurons connect to the mushroom body. According to the VFB database, downstream class-connectivity previews for adult thermosensory projection neurons include mushroom-body-associated dopaminergic neurons and gamma main Kenyon cells. This connectivity supports a plausible thermosensory influence on mushroom-body memory circuitry through thermosensory projection neurons, as stated in the VFB findings from VFB. 

VFB holds extensive data on both thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body, including images, subclasses, transgene expression, and connectivity classes, with, for example, [430](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005918,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for thermosensory neuron") downstream connectivity classes available for thermosensory neurons and [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") neurons with some part in the mushroom body. 

Temperature information could potentially influence memory formation given the connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body. This influence is plausible due to the connection between thermosensory projection neurons and mushroom-body-associated neurons, as indicated by the VFB evidence.

results.title: Data availability survey
results.question: I'm interested in studying the subesophageal zone (SEZ). How well-characterised is this region in VFB? What neuron types are annotated, what connectomics data is available, and what genetic tools exist for SEZ neurons?
results.response:
The [subesophageal zone](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00051068 "Open subesophageal zone in Virtual Fly Brain") is well-characterised in VFB, with various types of data available. There are [2698](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in subesophageal zone") neurons with some part in the subesophageal zone, including types such as [CB0550](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20004300 "Open CB0550 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [CB0552](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20004301 "Open CB0552 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [DSOG2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047702 "Open DSOG2 in Virtual Fly Brain"), [IB097](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20001274 "Open IB097 in Virtual Fly Brain"), and [SMP586](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_20003448 "Open SMP586 in Virtual Fly Brain"). The subesophageal zone is a neuropil mass below the esophagus, encompassing the three gnathal neuromeres and any regions of the cephalic neuromeres situated below the esophagus. 

In terms of connectomics data, VFB found 95 upstream class-connectivity partners for the [larval subesophageal zone](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00051067 "Open larval subesophageal zone in Virtual Fly Brain") vine neuron. 

For genetic tools, VFB returned 4205 genetic tool/expression pattern rows for the subesophageal zone, including GAL4 drivers and binary/intersectional drivers. This suggests a wide range of tools are available for studying SEZ neurons. 

VFB also holds data on parts of the subesophageal zone, with [122](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of subesophageal zone") records, as well as subclasses of the subesophageal zone, with [2](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of subesophageal zone") records. Additionally, there is [1](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00051068,ExpressionOverlapsHere "Run in VFB: Expression patterns overlapping subesophageal zone") record of expression patterns overlapping the subesophageal zone and 1 record of transgene expression in the subesophageal zone.
